newsitem.title: INDIA: El Nino unlikely to affect India's monsoon rains.
newsitem.headline: El Nino unlikely to affect India's monsoon rains.

text.p: El Nino warm water currents, showing an "unfavourable" trend this year, are unlikely to reduce India's monsoon rains substantially, a senior Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) official said on Wednesday.

A.V.R. Krishna Rao at the IMD told Reuters that the department had taken the El Nino factor into account while making the monsoon forecast in May. It had predicted that rainfall would be eight percent below the long-term average.
"Apart from that, I don't think El Nino will affect this years' monsoon," Rao said. "We stand by our forecast."
IMD has forecast a ninth sucessive normal monsoon in 1997.
El Nino raises the water temperature off the coast of South America and can disrupt weather patterns worldwide, creating drought conditions in some areas.
U.S. meteorologists have said the current El Nino is the strongest developing pattern since 1983 which could create drought conditions in many Asian countries.
Last month IMD officials had said that they would comment on El Nino's impact on monsoon rains in India only after seeing its progress through to the end of July.
Rao said the overall progress of monsoon rains was good and rains had covered most parts of India except some regions in northwestern regions.
"Some parts of Punjab and Haryana and Rajasthan have not been covered," Rao said.
But industry officials said the main rice growing areas of those states had received good rainfall, and sowing operations for the crop were in full swing.
The northern states of Punjab and Haryana are major rice and wheat producers.
"Rice farmers are happy in these regions," a senior offical in a leading foodgrains export firm told Reuters.
Rao said plentiful rainfall in southern India last week had made up for a slightly below par start to the monsoon in some parts of the south.
The southern states grow mainly oilseeds, coffee and rice.
Trade officials said that sowing for the oilseeds crop, which was delayed due to late rains, was going on at full tilt in the southern states of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
"The deficiency has been wiped off in some regions in central India also," Rao said. The central state of Madhya Pradesh account for 80 percent of the country's soybean output.
Coffee traders said that rains were satisfactory in the coffee growing belt in southern India although it was slightly delayed.
"Rainfall has been satisfactory in coffee growing areas," Arun Bidappa, an official in a leading coffee export firm.
But the humidity resulting from the delayed rains provided conditions for pests to breed.
"We will come to know the exact effect of pests in September when coffee beans are ready for harvest," Bidappa said.
